newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany's Kohl links political future to EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany's Kohl links political future to EMU.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, one of Europe's fiercest champions of closer European unity, on Friday linked his political future firmly to the success of the EU's planned single currency.
"I will tie my own political fate to the founding of the European currency union," the veteran chancellor told 800 bankers at the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt.

In Munich, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he wanted to stay at Kohl's side, telling a congress of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party: "We want to shape the path into the next century with Helmut Kohl at the helm."
The two statements highlighted the determination among Germany's political elite to see Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) project launched on schedule in 1999.

Kohl, who last month became Germany's longest serving post-war chancellor, has long said German and European unity were "two sides of the same coin." His Christian Democrats (CDU) now use that phrase to describe the mark and the euro.
As part of its drive for EMU, Kohl said that Germany, just like other nations, had to put its own house in order, slashing deficits and tearing down antiquated labour market structures.
"The goal must be that many nations meet the stability criteria and participate in the currency union from the start.
"Today it is important to map out the path for achieving this," Kohl added, stressing the "criteria in the Maastricht Treaty must be adhered to, in the long term as well."

European countries which want to meld their currencies in the Euro from 1999 are scrambling to meet economic criteria on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt laid down in the Maastricht agreement.

Most nations are facing great problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
Kohl made clear in his speech that countries which want to join EMU in 1999 must demonstrate that they can meet the Maastricht criteria over the long term and without excuses.
"The Maastricht criteria must be met without ifs and buts, and that means in the long term," he said.
Countering constant market speculation and suggestions that the Maastricht criteria could be watered down to allow more countries in, he said:
"When I am talking about criteria, I mean THE criteria. Anyone who thinks that we can turn away from this chosen path is deluding himself."
Waigel agreed in his Munich speech, saying: "We will not be party to an interpretive softening of the convergence criteria or to budgetary sleight-of-hand."
Kohl has recently drawn fire from unions as he has advocated putting the social welfare state on a diet as part of efforts to to pass the economic test for currency union.

But he noted that Bonn's plan to narrow next year's deficit to 53.3 billion marks ($35.5 billion) will move Germany closer to meeting the Maastricht Treaty deficit criteria of around three percent of the gross domestic product.

Kohl said Europe would stick by its stated goal of basing the decision on who made the grade for EMU on the basis of actual 1997 data -- meaning that estimates, forecasts and goals would not be taken into account.
"By then everyone should have swept his own doorstep and should refrain from pointing out others' failings," he said.

Brushing aside talk that the EMU timetable pressured countries to whip their finances into shape, putting economic growth at risk, Kohl said these efforts had to be made regardless of any ambitions to join the planned currency.
"We need to consolidate in any case, otherwise we would be paying the consequences until well into the next century," he said. ($1=1.5021 Mark)
